Language.String: José de San Martín (1778-1850) led the Andean crossing of 1817 and liberated Chile and Peru from Spanish rule — refusing political office to die in self-imposed European exile.\nThe Argentine Confederation grew from the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata into a federation of estancia provinces, dominated by the gaucho cavalry and the Buenos Aires merchant class.

Hayreddin Barbarossa (c.1478-1546), Ottoman corsair turned Kapudan Pasha, ruled Algiers and commanded the imperial fleet's Mediterranean victories at Preveza and beyond.\nThe Regency of Algiers and its Tripoli/Tunis sister-states were Ottoman corsair principalities — the Barbary States — raiding European shipping for slaves and tribute until the 19th century.

Dom Pedro I (1798-1834), born in Lisbon and regent of Brazil from 1821, uttered the Grito do Ipiranga on 7 September 1822 and declared Brazilian independence — becoming the first Emperor of Brazil; in 1831 he abdicated to return to Portugal and defend his daughter Queen Maria II's throne.\nThe Brazilian Empire's Distributed Economic Network doctrine spread Mills, Plantations, and Markets across the pampa frontier, sustaining Hessian reserve infantry and the mounted imperial cavalry with a ceaseless trickle of colonial revenue.

Mariano Vallejo (1808-1890), Californio commander at Sonoma, was captured by the 1846 Bear Flag insurgents but later helped draft California's state constitution.\nThe California Republic — the Bear Flag revolt — declared independence at Sonoma in 1846, lasting only weeks before US annexation in the Mexican-American War.

Sir Isaac Brock (1769-1812), born on Guernsey and dubbed the Saviour of Upper Canada, captured Fort Detroit in August 1812 alongside Tecumseh before falling at Queenston Heights — knighted posthumously for his defence of British North America.\nThe Canadians field a doctrine of frontier militia, Indigenous alliances, and early aggressive action, wielding compact regulars and settler levies to punish overextension on the Great Lakes frontier.

Francisco Morazán (1792-1842), liberal Honduran general, led the Federal Republic of Central America's defense before being executed by Costa Rican conservatives.\nThe Federal Republic of Central America (1823-1841) was a brief liberal federation of Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua and Costa Rica that fractured into the modern republics.

Bernardo O'Higgins (1778-1842) co-led the Andean campaign with San Martín and served as Chile's Supreme Director (1817-1823), instituting the new republic's military and constitution.\nThe Republic of Chile defended itself from royalist counter-attacks and, in the 1879-83 War of the Pacific, seized the nitrate-rich Atacama from Bolivia and Peru.

Simón Bolívar (1783-1830), El Libertador, freed six South American nations from Spain and dreamt the unfulfilled Gran Colombia — president of Venezuela, Peru, and the brief federation.\nGran Colombia (1819-1831) bound modern Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and Panamá in Bolívar's federal vision before regional caudillos shattered it apart.

Muhammad Ali Pasha (r. 1805-1848), Albanian-Ottoman mercenary turned ruler, modernised Egypt with conscription, cotton, French advisors, and the elimination of the Mamluks at the Citadel massacre.\nThe Khedivate of Egypt (1867-1914) was nominally Ottoman but built the Suez Canal, fielded a modern conscript army, and fell to British de-facto occupation after the 1882 Urabi revolt.

Juan Bautista Alvarado (1809-1882), Californio governor, declared the short-lived 1836 Free State of Alta California — the seed of later northern Mexican autonomist movements.\nThe Free State of Baja California sprang from Californio resistance to Mexican centralism — desert mission ranchos, vaquero cavalry, and pearl-fishing harbours from La Paz to San José.

Carl Gustaf Mannerheim (1867-1951) — Tsarist general turned Finnish marshal — led the White army in the 1918 Civil War and the Finnish defence in the Winter and Continuation Wars.\nThe Grand Duchy of Finland (1809-1917) was an autonomous Russian dominion that nurtured Finnish national identity through the Kalevala, Sibelius, and the eventual 1917 declaration of independence.

Louis Riel (1844-1885) led the Métis in the Red River Resistance and the North-West Rebellion, founding Manitoba before his execution by the Canadian government.\nLower Canada was the French-speaking Catholic society of the St. Lawrence valley, anchored on the seigneurial system and the 1837 Patriote uprising for responsible government.

Toussaint L'Ouverture (c.1743-1803), self-emancipated former slave, led the only successful slave revolution in modern history and effectively founded Haiti before dying in a Napoleonic prison.\nThe First Empire of Haiti (1804) was the world's first Black-led republic born of the only successful slave revolt — a defiant anti-colonial state on the western third of Hispaniola.

Lajos Kossuth (1802-1894), governor-president of revolutionary Hungary in 1848-49, led the brief independence war against Habsburg Austria before defeat by Russian intervention.\nThe Kingdom of Hungary endured Ottoman partition, Habsburg Compromise (1867), and the post-Trianon truncation — built on Magyar nobility, Pannonian agriculture, and the hussar tradition.

Prince Diponegoro (1785-1855), Javanese aristocrat and Sufi mystic, led the 1825-30 Java War against Dutch colonial rule that killed perhaps 200,000 Javanese.\nThe Sultanate of Yogyakarta — central court of Java — preserved royal Mataram-Sultanate culture under Dutch suzerainty, with kris, gamelan, and the dual sultan-and-pangeran nobility.

Jacinto Pat and Cecilio Chi launched the 1847 Caste War — referenced here through Canek, the spirit of the Cruzob holy-cross movement that ruled rebel Maya territory until 1901.\nThe Cruzob Maya state (1850-1901) of Chan Santa Cruz fought the Caste War against the Yucatec ladinos for over half a century — sustained by the Talking Cross oracle and British arms from Belize.

Andrés de Santa Cruz (1792-1865), Mestizo general and Peru-Bolivia Confederation founder, fought through Junín and Ayacucho in the wars of independence before the confederation collapsed in 1839.\nThe Republic of Peru rose on Lima's wealth and Andean silver, lurched through caudillo wars, lost the War of the Pacific to Chile, and endured the long civilismo era.

Starting in the 17th Century from small settlements like those of Jamestown and Plymouth, British of various backgrounds moved to the New World and organized themselves into 13 Colonies stretching the eastern coast of North America. Following the Seven Years War, the British Parliment levied additional taxes upon the colonists to try and recouperate its cost, without the assent of the colonies. These and other grievences convinced most of the American elite that Independence was prefferable, and with the eventual assistance of France and Spain fought and won that right.

Napoleon Bonaparte (1769-1821) crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804 and conquered most of continental Europe before disastrous defeats in Russia (1812) and at Waterloo (1815).\nThe French Empire welded the Revolution's reforms onto a centralised military meritocracy — Code Napoléon, the Grande Armée, and a Continental System aimed at strangling Britain.

France — begins as the Revolutionary Republic under Robespierre, and may rise as Napoleon's First Empire.\nMaximilien Robespierre (1758-1794) led the Republic through levée-en-masse conscription and the Reign of Terror. At Age III, choose the "Coronation of Napoleon" politician to transform into the First French Empire, unlocking the Imperial Old Guard, Grand Battery, and the Continental Blockade.

Spanish explorers had only discovered the east coast of Mexico in 1518, but by 1521 rouge conquistador Hernan Cortez had conquered the Aztec Empire with the help of locals subjegated by the Aztecs. Based in Mexico city, this colony dubbed the Viceroyalty of New Spain slowly expanded from California to Panama over the next two centuries, along the way fighting various native tribes as well as rival European powers. With Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808, Mexican elites siezed the moment to argue for home rule. The next 70 years were marked by political instability, civil war, and revolution.

Antonio Canales Rosillo (1802-1869), Tamaulipas federalist colonel, led the 1840 Republic of the Rio Grande secession against Santa Anna's centralist regime.\nThe Republic of the Rio Grande (1840) declared independence for Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas — a federalist Mexican breakaway crushed within ten months of its founding.

Alexandru Ioan Cuza (1820-1873) merged Wallachia and Moldavia in 1859 to found the United Principalities, abolishing serfdom before his deposition by the Monstrous Coalition.\nThe United Romanian Principalities became an independent kingdom in 1881 after the Russo-Turkish War, blending Latin Orthodox heritage with the Carpathian frontier.

Paul Kruger (1825-1904), President of the South African Republic, led the Boers in the Second Boer War (1899-1902) against the British Empire before exile in Switzerland.\nThe South African Republic (Transvaal) was a Boer pioneer state of trekkers, gold from Witwatersrand, and laagered ox-wagon defence — overrun by the British during the South African War.

Sam Houston (1793-1863) defeated Santa Anna at San Jacinto in 1836 and twice served as President of the Republic of Texas before its annexation by the United States.\nThe Republic of Texas (1836-1846) wrested independence from Mexico at San Jacinto and held a Lone Star nation across the Comanche frontier until annexation by the United States.

Felipe Carrillo Puerto (1874-1924), Mayan-speaking Yucatecan socialist governor, championed indigenous land reform until assassinated by reactionaries.\nThe Republic of Yucatán declared independence twice (1841-43, 1846-48) over Mexican centralism — only the Caste War of the Maya forced reincorporation in exchange for federal aid.

Maximilien Robespierre (1758-1794) led the Committee of Public Safety through the levée-en-masse mobilization and the Reign of Terror — toppled by Thermidorian reaction on 9 Thermidor Year II.\nThe First French Republic (1792-1804) transformed feudal armies into citizen-soldiers, fielding the largest force in European history through civic nationalism, forced requisition, and the principle that merit — not birth — was the path to command.

Usman dan Fodio (1754-1817) led the 1804 Fulani jihad that overthrew the Hausa city-state kings and founded the Sokoto Caliphate centred on his son Muhammad Bello.\nThe Sokoto Caliphate (1804-1903) bound the Hausaland city-states under Sharia governance, slave-cavalry warfare, and trans-Saharan caravan trade until the British conquest.
Ivan the Terrible

Ivan IV the Terrible (r. 1547-1584) crowned himself first Tsar of All Rus', conquered Kazan and Astrakhan, and unleashed the Oprichnik terror to break the boyars.\nTsarist Russia welded together the Streltsy musketeer corps, vast peasant levies, and Orthodox missionary expansion across the Eurasian frontier.
Maurice of Nassau

Maurice of Nassau (r. 1585-1625) modernised European warfare with drilled musket lines, modular fortification, and the precise pay-and-supply that made his army a match for Spain.\nThe Dutch Republic ran the 17th-century world economy through the Bank of Amsterdam and the East-India Company (VOC), trading from New Amsterdam to Batavia.
Menelik II

Menelik II (r. 1889-1913) crushed the Italian invasion at Adwa in 1896, securing Ethiopian independence and modernising the empire from Addis Ababa.\nThe Ethiopian Empire repelled European colonisation alone in Africa, fielding Solomonic monarchy, Coptic Christianity, and the highland fortress system.
Shivaji Maharaj

Chhatrapati Shivaji Bhonsle (1630-1680), crowned at Raigad in 1674, forged the Maratha kingdom from the Sahyadri hill-forts using ganimi kava — swift raid-and-withdraw cavalry tactics — and famously escaped Aurangzeb's court at Agra to deny Mughal conquest.\nThe Maratha Confederacy (1674-1818) that Shivaji fathered spread from Pune to the Himalayas, wielding light cavalry, hill-fort networks, and confederate Peshwa statecraft to eclipse the Mughal Empire.
Montezuma II

Motecuhzoma II Xocoyotzin (r. 1502-1520) presided over the Aztec Triple Alliance at its territorial zenith and was killed during the Spanish entrada of Cortés.\nThe Aztec Triple Alliance bound Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan in tribute confederation; Xochiyaoyotl 'flower wars' fed the captive economy of Templo Mayor.
Pachacuti

Túpac Inca Yupanqui (r. 1471-1493) — and the broader Sapa Inca line — pushed Tawantinsuyu to its fullest extent across the Andes from Quito to Santiago.\nThe Inca Empire integrated four suyus along the qhapaq-ñan road network, terraced agriculture, mit'a labor tax, and quipu accounting — without a written language or wheel.
Isabella I of Castile

Isabella I of Castile (r. 1474-1504) co-ruled with Ferdinand of Aragon, expelled the Moors at Granada, and personally chartered Columbus's 1492 voyage.\nThe Spanish Empire of the Habsburgs and early Bourbons drew silver from Potosí and Mexico, fielded the Tercio infantry square, and converted the New World by sword and missionary.
Louis XVIII

Louis XVIII (r. 1814-1815, 1815-1824) reclaimed the Bourbon throne after Napoleon's fall, balancing Restoration legitimism with grudging concessions to revolutionary reforms.\nBourbon France revolved around the Sun King's grand court, the dragoon and gendarmerie tradition, and the Catholic Ancien Régime that the Revolution would later overthrow.
Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla

Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla (1753-1811) raised the Grito de Dolores in 1810 against Spain, igniting the Mexican War of Independence — though executed before its 1821 victory.\nThe First Mexican Empire rose from Hidalgo and Iturbide's revolt, oscillating between centralist conservative and liberal-federal regimes through Texas, the Mexican-American War, and Maximilian.
George Washington

George Washington (1732-1799) commanded the Continental Army to victory over Britain in 1781 and became first President of the United States in 1789.\nThe early United States expanded westward via the Northwest Ordinance, the Louisiana Purchase, and Manifest Destiny — a republic of yeoman farmers, militia, and Atlantic merchants.
Prince Henry the Navigator

Prince Henry the Navigator (1394-1460) sponsored the great Atlantic-coast expeditions out of Sagres, opening the route around Africa toward the Indian Ocean spice trade.\nPortugal pioneered Europe's age of discovery — Brazil, Goa, Macau, and the African slave-trade triangle all flowed through Lisbon's caravel-and-carrack fleets.
Giuseppe Garibaldi

Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807-1882) led the Mille Redshirts through Sicily and Naples in 1860, decisively unifying southern Italy under Vittorio Emanuele II.\nThe Kingdom of Italy (1861-1946) wove Risorgimento republicans, Sardinian monarchists and the Pope's reluctant Romans into a single Latin nation-state.
Gustavus Adolphus

Gustavus Adolphus (r. 1611-1632), the Lion of the North, revolutionised European warfare with combined arms — light cannon, salvo musket fire and Hakkapelit cavalry — until his death at Lützen.\nThe Swedish Empire (1611-1721) rose to dominate the Baltic on the Carolean line-infantry doctrine before falling to Peter the Great's Russia at Poltava.
Jean Parisot de Valette

Jean Parisot de Valette (1494-1568), Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller, led the heroic defence of Malta in the 1565 Great Siege against Ottoman besiegers.\nThe Order of Saint John ruled Malta (1530-1798) as a corsair-and-fortress state — Hospitaller crusaders bound by triple vows, funded by piracy on Ottoman shipping.
Kangxi Emperor

The Kangxi Emperor (r. 1661-1722) of the Qing Dynasty consolidated Manchu rule over China, defeated the Three Feudatories, and patronised the great Qing-era encyclopedias and atlases.\nQing Dynasty China commanded the world's largest population and economy, with the Eight Banners army, Confucian bureaucracy, and Forbidden City court at its centre.
Suleiman the Magnificent

Suleiman I (r. 1520-1566), the 10th Ottoman Sultan — "the Magnificent" to Western Europe, "Kanuni" the Lawgiver to his own people — conquered Belgrade (1521), Rhodes (1522), and crushed Hungary at Mohács (1526) before besieging Vienna in 1529, while reforming the empire's legal code.\nThe Ottoman Siege Train Concentration doctrine pairs Janissary infantry and sipahi cavalry with an overwhelming battery of heavy bombards, grinding forward in slow siege columns behind stone walls to project the Sublime Porte's gunpowder supremacy.
Tokugawa Ieyasu

Tokugawa Ieyasu (r. 1603-1605 as shogun) ended the Sengoku wars at Sekigahara in 1600 and founded the Tokugawa shogunate, which closed Japan to most foreigners for 250 years.\nEdo-period Japan was Sakoku — peace under the Tokugawa shogunate, samurai-bureaucrat governance, and the rising chonin merchant culture of Edo and Osaka.
Hiawatha

Hiawatha, with the Peacemaker Deganawida, founded the Haudenosaunee Confederacy (the Five Nations) in pre-contact times, binding the Iroquois nations under the Great Law of Peace.\nThe Haudenosaunee Confederacy of Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca governed by clan-mother council, dominated the Eastern Woodlands fur trade, and played England and France against each other.
Chief Gall

Phizí — Chief Gall (c. 1840-1894), Hunkpapa Lakota war chief and Sitting Bull's principal field commander — led the main cavalry charge that shattered Custer's 7th Cavalry at Little Bighorn on June 25, 1876, fighting with a fury sharpened by soldiers killing his family in 1865.\nThe Lakota Sioux were Plains horse warriors whose fluid, terrain-driven raids and disciplined mass charges dominated the Northern Plains, striking hard and dispersing before any counter-blow could land.
Frederick the Great

Frederick the Great of Prussia (r. 1740-1786) drilled the Prussian army into Europe's most precise instrument and won Silesia from Habsburg Austria with oblique-order tactics.\nThe German Empire (1871-1918) unified the German-speaking states under Hohenzollern Prussia, fielding the precision Prussian army, conscript Reichsheer, and the industrial Krupp arsenal.

Always outnumbered, never outfought. We march.
You are neither Austrian nor French. I shall have to improvise.
Bastions, sally ports, covered ways. Vauban's geometry, Prussian discipline.
Walls delay. They do not deny. Silesia still answers to Berlin.
A Hussar lost. His regiment continues without him.
Oblique order. Concentration at the flank. The Austrian army folds as designed.
För Gud och fäderneslandet. God and fatherland — we march together.
The Lion of the North is abroad. Kneel or face the Hakkapeliitta.
Stockholm's core holds. The Carolean redoubts ring the approach.
Walls? I brought cannon. Walls are a matter of patience.
A brave Swede lost. His widow will have the Crown's purse.
As at Breitenfeld — combined arms, light cannon, cavalry flank. The day is ours.
The six fires burn together. We speak with one voice.
You have not learned the Great Law. We will teach you.
The longhouse stands, the palisade rises. The village will be whole.
He hides as a weak brother would. The Confederacy does not hide.
A warrior has gone to the Great Peace. We sing his name tonight.
The circle closes. The Great Law is older than this war.
Stand with the Tsar. The Oprichnina does not forget loyalty.
Traitor — Moscow tolerates no rival. Your lands shall be ash.
The Kremlin's walls rise. Let them dash themselves upon stone.
He cowers. Even cowards must answer to the rod.
A faithful servant slain. His killers will be hunted to the steppes.
God's will. The earth bows to Moscow as it must.
A good day to ride together. Hoka hey.
You have come to the Paha Sapa. You will not leave.
The Lakota do not wall. The camp moves.
He builds walls. He has forgotten how to fight.
A brother rides the spirit trail. Today is a good day.
As at the Greasy Grass — the cavalry rode in, and did not ride out.
O Roma, o morte! With you, comrade, we make Italy.
I have fought kings and popes. You are no worse than either.
The Risorgimento holds its cities, block by block.
Another tyrant behind stone. The Redshirts will climb his wall.
A Redshirt fallen. Italy remembers her sons.
Mille cammie rosse — and one more victory for the nation.
The sea is wide and the horizons are ours. We sail together.
I have charted stranger shores than you. Your coast, too, will be known.
Sagres stands on the cliff. The harbor is walled, the sea is open.
He walls the land. I command the sea. The sea wins.
A sailor lost. The ocean takes and gives.
The caravel returns victorious. New shores, new victories.
¡Viva la Virgen de Guadalupe! Caminamos juntos.
¡El Grito de Dolores! Spain will hear us from the pulpit itself.
La Alhóndiga stands. The iglesias become fortresses when the Republic calls.
A gachupín hides. Our machetes do not tire.
Un hijo de Dolores ha caído. The Republic honors him.
¡Por la independencia! The parish rises, the viceroy's men fall.
For Crown and Cross, we ride as one. God wills it.
Granada fell. Then Iberia. Then the New World. Do not be the next line.
The alcázar holds. No Moor, no heretic shall pass.
Walls do not save those who oppose the true faith.
A hidalgo gave his life. He dies in grace.
As at the Reconquista — the Cross advances, the field is ours.
For the Order and for the Faith. We stand together.
The Turk came to Malta and left his bones. You shall not do better.
Birgu, Senglea, St. Elmo. Three rings of stone and the will of God.
Walls. The Hospitaller knows walls better than any man alive.
A knight falls into God's hand. We mourn and continue.
As at the Great Siege — the Turk broke, the Order held. Deo gratias.
The Son of Heaven greets his ally. The Mandate runs through both our hands.
The Qing do not address barbarians twice. Kneel, or depart.
The Great Wall was built for such moments. Stone and patience prevail.
Barbarian walls crumble before imperial cannon. It has ever been so.
A banner-servant is lost. His family is entered in the Imperial register.
The Eight Banners prevail, as the Mandate requires. Order is restored.
By drill and discipline, my friend. The Dutch way.
You have not studied the line. You will learn.
The polders flood, the walls stand. The Republic holds.
Even stone yields to persistence. Mark his weakness.
A good officer, gone. Send word to his city.
Volley and counter-march. They broke as drilled men expected.
Abyssinia greets her friends. We fight together for the highland.
Adwa is not yet finished. Come and see.
The amba is a wall by nature. The stone is only for the gate.
A foreigner building walls on our earth. Let him build his grave.
A son of the highland falls. We do not forget.
As at Adwa: the mountain does not bow. The field is ours.
The gods smile on this alliance. Their blood binds ours.
The smoking mirror shows me your end. Come, meet it.
The chinampas float. The causeways guard. Tenochtitlan endures.
He walls as if the jaguar could not climb. Foolish.
An offering. The sun drinks. We continue.
The flower war ends in victory. As the calendar foretold.
Soldiers! Forty centuries look down upon us. We march together.
Impossible is a word only found in the dictionary of fools.
Marshal, field fortifications only. The Grande Armée advances, not hides.
He builds walls. Excellent — his army will be delivered to us like pastry.
Un officier brave est tombé. We avenge him with French arms.
As at Austerlitz — surprise them on the flank, and the Empire takes another page.
Viracocha sees our alliance. The Four Suyus stand with you.
You are far from your sea. The mountain will teach you.
The stones of Sacsayhuamán fit without mortar. As the land itself.
A lowlander building walls in the highland. The altitude is his enemy before I am.
A son of Inti falls. The ancestors remember.
As the Inca hand built Cusco: patient, stone by stone. Victory follows.
We hold these truths self-evident. And we hold this line together.
The tree of liberty must be refreshed from time to time. Prepare to water it.
The frontier blockhouse. Wood, powder, and the will of free men.
Tyranny behind stone. A republic will find the cracks.
A yeoman fallen. His farm shall be honored.
As at Yorktown — the citizen-soldier prevails when the cause is just.
